balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Waters Corporation: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Waters Corporation: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Waters Corporation: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Waters Corporation: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Waters Corporation: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Waters Corporation: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Waters Corporation: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue (post-BDS structure)
segmentRevenue.content:
Waters closed a Reverse Morris Trust acquisition of Becton, Dickinson's Biosciences & Diagnostic Solutions (BDS) business on 9 February 2026, roughly doubling revenue and replacing the old two-segment structure (Waters, TA Instruments) with three: Analytical & Materials Sciences (legacy Waters + TA Instruments), Biosciences (ex-BD flow cytometry, single-cell multiomics, reagents) and Advanced Diagnostics (ex-BD microbiology/molecular diagnostics plus legacy Waters clinical).

For Waters Corporation: only Q1-Q3 2026 carry all three new segments; FY2025 and earlier periods predate the deal and are blank here -- compare them using the legacy Revenue/RecurringRevenue charts instead, not this one.

What to watch:

  • Whether Biosciences and Advanced Diagnostics sustain the growth rates management guided to at the deal's close
  • Integration costs and dis-synergies showing up in Analytical & Materials Sciences margin before segment-level margins are disclosed
  • Mix shift: diagnostics and biosciences are lower-margin, higher-growth than the legacy instrument business

revenueMix.title: Revenue by type: instruments vs consumables vs service
revenueMix.content:
Instrument revenue is the one-time capital-equipment sale; consumables (columns, reagents, assay kits) and service (maintenance, software) are the recurring, repeat-purchase tail that follows every instrument placement.

For Waters Corporation: this is the legacy razor/razor-blade split the RecurringRevenuePct KPI card summarizes as one number -- consumables plus service has run well over half of revenue historically, and the mix is the lead indicator for the installed base, not the headline revenue line.

What to watch:

  • Instrument revenue growth, since it funds future consumables/service growth with a lag
  • Consumables and service holding up even when instrument capex cycles turn down (pharma/biotech capital spending is cyclical)
  • Whether the BDS-acquired businesses (diagnostics assay kits, reagents) carry the same recurring characteristics once reported into this split

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Waters Corporation: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Waters Corporation: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
